title: A Passage to Africa
author: George Alagiah
blurb: War reporting from Somalia that questions the ethics of journalism and confronts uncomfortable truths about watching human suffering.
source: Extract from A Passage to Africa (2001)
heading: A Passage to Africa

paragraphs.html: I saw a thousand hungry, lean, scared and betrayed faces as I criss-crossed Somalia between the end of 1991 and December 1992, but there is one I will never forget.

I was in a little hamlet just outside Gufgaduud, a village in the back of beyond, a place the aid agencies had yet to reach. In my notebook I had jotted down instructions on how to get there. 'Take the Badale Road for a few kilometres till the end of the tarmac, turn right on to a dirt track, stay on it for about forty-five minutes — Gufgaduud. Go another fifteen minutes approx. — like a ghost village.'

In the ghoulish manner of journalists on the hunt for the most striking pictures, my cameraman and I tramped from one hut to another. What might have appalled us when we'd started our trip just a few days before no longer impressed us much. The search for the shocking is like the craving for a drug: you require heavier and more frequent doses the longer you're at it. Pictures that stun the editors one day are written off as the same old stuff the next. This sounds callous, but it is just a fact of life. It's how we collect and compile the images that so move people in the comfort of their sitting rooms back home.

There was Amina Abdirahman, who had gone out that morning in search of wild, edible roots, leaving her two young girls lying on the dirt floor of their hut. They had been sick for days, and were reaching the final, enervating stages of terminal hunger. Habiba was ten years old and her sister, Ayaan, was nine. By the time Amina returned, she had only one daughter. Habiba had died. No rage, no whimpering, just a passing away — that simple, frictionless, motionless deliverance from a state of half-life to death itself. It was, as I said at the time in my dispatch, a vision of 'famine away from the headlines, a famine of quiet suffering and lonely death'.

There was the old woman who lay in her hut, abandoned by relations who were too weak to carry her on their journey to find food. It was the smell that drew me to her doorway: the smell of decaying flesh. Where her shinbone should have been there was a festering wound the size of my hand. She'd been shot in the leg as the retreating army of the deposed dictator took revenge on whoever it found in its way. The shattered leg had fused into the gentle V-shape of a boomerang. It was rotting; she was rotting. You could see it in her sick, yellow eyes and smell it in the putrid air she recycled with every struggling breath she took.
And then there was the face I will never forget.

My reaction to everyone else I met that day was a mixture of pity and revulsion. Yes, revulsion. The degeneration of the human body, sucked of its natural vitality by the twin evils of hunger and disease, is a disgusting thing. We never say so in our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached. To be in a feeding centre is to hear and smell the excretion of fluids by people who are beyond controlling their bodily functions. To be in a feeding centre is surreptitiously to wipe your hands on the back of your trousers after you've held the clammy palm of a mother who has just cleaned vomit from her child's mouth.

There's pity, too, because even in this state of utter despair they aspire to a dignity that is almost impossible to achieve. An old woman will cover her shrivelled body with a soiled cloth as your gaze turns towards her. Or the old and dying man who keeps his hoe next to the mat with which, one day soon, they will shroud his corpse, as if he means to go out and till the soil once all this is over.

I saw that face for only a few seconds, a fleeting meeting of eyes before the face turned away, as its owner retreated into the darkness of another hut. In those brief moments there had been a smile, not from me, but from the face. It was not a smile of greeting, it was not a smile of joy — how could it be? — but it was a smile nonetheless. It touched me in a way I could not explain. It moved me in a way that went beyond pity or revulsion.

What was it about that smile? I had to find out. I urged my translator to ask the man why he had smiled. He came back with an answer. 'It's just that he was embarrassed to be found in this condition,' the translator explained. And then it clicked. That's what the smile had been about. It was the feeble smile that goes with apology, the kind of smile you might give if you felt you had done something wrong.

Normally inured to stories of suffering, accustomed to the evidence of deprivation, I was unsettled by this one smile in a way I had never been before. There is an unwritten code between the journalist and his subjects in these situations. The journalist observes, the subject is observed. The journalist is active, the subject is passive. But this smile had turned the tables on that tacit agreement. Without uttering a single word, the man had posed a question that cut to the heart of the relationship between me and him, between us and them, between the rich world and the poor world. If he was embarrassed to be found weakened by hunger and ground down by conflict, how should I feel to be standing there so strong and confident?

I resolved there and then that I would write the story of Gufgaduud with all the power and purpose I could muster. It seemed at the time, and still does, the only adequate answer a reporter can give to the man's question.

I have one regret about that brief encounter in Gufgaduud. Having searched through my notes and studied the dispatch that the BBC broadcast, I see that I never found out what the man's name was. Yet meeting him was a seminal moment in the gradual collection of experiences we call context. Facts and figures are the easy part of journalism. Knowing where they sit in the great scheme of things is much harder. So, my nameless friend, if you are still alive, I owe you one.

a1.quote: I saw a thousand hungry, lean, scared and betrayed faces
a1.what: 'hungry, lean, scared and betrayed' builds from physical to emotional. 'Betrayed' carries by far the greatest weight as the final, unexpected term — it implies human agency and political failure behind the suffering, not merely natural disaster.

a2.quote: Somalia between the end of 1991 and December 1992,
a2.what: Somalia collapsed into civil war in 1991 after the fall of dictator Siad Barre. Rival warlords fought for power while a famine — made far worse by the conflict — killed an estimated 300,000 people. George Alagiah was one of the BBC's most prominent foreign correspondents; this extract is from his memoir A Passage to Africa (2001), written a decade after the events.

a3.what: The piece opens with 'I' — immediately establishing this as personal testimony rather than news report. Alagiah positions himself as witness, not just correspondent, which changes the reader's relationship to what follows.

a4.gist: What does this opening make you expect?
a4.what: 'There is one I will never forget' — how does this opening affect your expectations as a reader? What kind of piece are you prepared for — an objective news report, or something more personal? Does the promise of something unforgettable make you trust Alagiah before he has said anything of substance?

a5.quote: a village in the back of beyond,
a5.what: 'a village in the back of beyond' is deliberately casual, almost throwaway. Its informality contrasts with the horror that follows — a writer managing his emotional response through understatement.

a7.quote: the aid agencies had yet to reach.
a7.what: International organisations such as UNICEF, the Red Cross, and Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) were attempting to reach famine victims across Somalia. The scale of the crisis overwhelmed relief efforts, and many rural areas went weeks or months without any outside assistance. Journalists like Alagiah were sometimes the first outsiders to reach remote communities.

a6.quote: a place the aid agencies had yet to reach. In my notebook I had jotted down instructions on how to get there.
a6.what: The casual register here — 'back of beyond', 'jotted down', 'approx.' — reveals a voice that controls its emotion through deliberate informality. This is a professional managing distress with deadpan language, which makes the horror that breaks through all the more powerful.

a8.quote: Take the Badale Road for a few kilometres till the end of the tarmac, turn right on to a dirt track, stay on it for about forty-five minutes — Gufgaduud. Go another fifteen minutes approx. — like a ghost village.
a8.what: Quoting directly from his notebook creates authenticity — the reader feels they are following a real route. The clipped, practical language of the directions contrasts sharply with what Alagiah finds at their end.

a9.what: Why does Alagiah include the actual directions from his notebook? What does quoting 'approx.' and 'like a ghost village' do to the reader? Consider how this creates a sense of following him into a place the reader would never otherwise reach.

a10.quote: In the ghoulish manner of journalists on the hunt for the most striking pictures,
a10.what: 'In the ghoulish manner of journalists' — Alagiah opens by implicating himself in something predatory. This is an unusual and risky move for a journalist writing about his own work. It establishes a voice that prioritises honesty over self-image.

a11.quote: What might have appalled us when we'd started our trip just a few days before no longer impressed us much.
a11.what: 'What might have appalled us when we'd started our trip just a few days before no longer impressed us much.' Alagiah quietly admits that a few days of exposure have already dulled his responses. This is honest and uncomfortable — he is showing us how the professional mind adapts in ways that are morally troubling.

a12.quote: The search for the shocking is like the craving for a drug: you require heavier and more frequent doses the longer you're at it.
a12.what: 'The search for the shocking is like the craving for a drug: you require heavier and more frequent doses the longer you're at it.' Comparing journalism to addiction implies moral compromise and loss of control. The second person 'you' broadens the accusation beyond Alagiah, implicating the reader too.

a13.quote: This sounds callous, but it is just a fact of life.
a13.what: 'you require heavier and more frequent doses' — the shift to second person makes the reader complicit. Are we part of the audience that consumes disaster images from 'the comfort of their sitting rooms'? Alagiah is not only confessing on behalf of journalists; he is also pointing at us. How does this make you feel toward him, and toward yourself?

a14.quote: It's how we collect and compile the images that so move people in the comfort of their sitting rooms back home.
a14.what: 'people in the comfort of their sitting rooms back home' — who does this phrase describe? Where are you reading this? Alagiah creates a deliberate contrast between the extreme reality of Somalia and the comfort of those who consume images of it. Does this phrase make you feel implicated, or separated from the events?

a15.what: Naming the individuals — Amina Abdirahman, Habiba, Ayaan — resists the anonymity that dehumanises victims. The names are given in full, with dignity. Compare ¶13, where Alagiah admits he never learned the man's name — the one who affected him most.

a16.quote: Habiba was ten years old and her sister, Ayaan, was nine.
a16.what: 'Habiba was ten years old and her sister, Ayaan, was nine.' Why does Alagiah give us the exact ages? How does this specificity affect your emotional response? Consider how different it would feel if he had simply written 'two young girls'.

a17.quote: No rage, no whimpering, just a passing away — that simple, frictionless, motionless deliverance from a state of half-life to death itself.
a17.what: 'No rage, no whimpering, just a passing away — that simple, frictionless, motionless deliverance from a state of half-life to death itself.' Parallel negatives slow the pace to match the stillness of death. 'Frictionless' and 'motionless' are clinical, almost scientific — quietly devastating.

a18.quote: It was, as I said at the time in my dispatch, a vision of
a18.what: The language here is restrained almost to the point of coldness — 'frictionless', 'motionless', 'deliverance'. This is not sentimentality but professional control over material that is devastating. The restraint itself signals the depth of what Alagiah is suppressing.

a19.quote: 'famine away from the headlines, a famine of quiet suffering and lonely death'.
a19.what: Quoting his own earlier broadcast words draws attention to the gap between lived experience and finished journalism. 'A famine of quiet suffering and lonely death' is fine writing — but Alagiah is also aware that it is crafted language applied to real pain. This self-consciousness runs through the whole piece.

a20.quote: abandoned by relations who were too weak to carry her on their journey to find food.
a20.what: 'abandoned by relations who were too weak to carry her' — Alagiah is careful to contextualise the abandonment. The relatives did not leave out of cruelty; they were 'too weak'. This is the voice of a journalist who resists simple moral judgements, insisting on the complexity of extreme circumstances.

a21.quote: It was the smell that drew me to her doorway: the smell of decaying flesh.
a21.what: 'It was the smell that drew me to her doorway: the smell of decaying flesh.' Repeating 'smell' is deliberate. The senses override choice — Alagiah is pulled helplessly toward suffering he can do nothing about. Smell is the hardest sense to ignore or aestheticise.

a22.quote: a festering wound the size of my hand.
a22.what: 'a festering wound the size of my hand' — using his own body as a unit of measurement makes the abstract injury viscerally real. It also implicates Alagiah physically in what he describes.

a23.quote: the retreating army of the deposed dictator
a23.what: As Siad Barre's government collapsed, retreating soldiers committed widespread atrocities against civilians. Alagiah is careful to name the perpetrators — 'the retreating army of the deposed dictator' — rather than allowing the suffering to appear natural or inevitable. This is a political account as well as a humanitarian one.

a24.quote: It was rotting; she was rotting.
a24.what: 'It was rotting; she was rotting.' The semi-colon creates a horrifying equivalence between the wound and the woman. The repetition collapses the distinction between body and injury — she is becoming indistinguishable from her own decay.

a25.quote: You could see it in her sick, yellow eyes and smell it in the putrid air she recycled with every struggling breath she took.
a25.gist: Limits of sympathy — how does this paragraph affect you?
a25.what: Alagiah will shortly admit to feeling 'revulsion' as well as pity. Before reading that admission — how do you respond to the description of the old woman? Do you feel only sympathy, or something else too? What does your own reaction tell you about Alagiah's purpose in writing this paragraph so graphically?

a26.quote: And then there was the face I will never forget.
a26.what: A single sentence given its own paragraph. After the accumulation of horrors in ¶¶3–5, this acts as a structural hinge — returning to the opening promise and signalling a tonal shift. The isolation gives it enormous weight on the page.

a27.gist: Structural effect of the one-sentence paragraph
a27.what: This single sentence is given its own paragraph. How does this affect the pace of your reading? After three dense paragraphs of accumulated horror, what does this isolation signal? Does it create anticipation, relief, or unease?

a28.what: 'Yes, revulsion.' The one-word sentence catches Alagiah being honest when honesty is professionally uncomfortable. Journalists are not expected to admit finding their subjects repulsive. The bluntness performs the confession without any attempt at mitigation.

a29.quote: The degeneration of the human body, sucked of its natural vitality by the twin evils of hunger and disease, is a disgusting thing.
a29.what: Alagiah admits to feeling revulsion toward starving, dying people. This is a deeply uncomfortable thing to read. Does his admission make him seem honest and trustworthy, or does it disturb you? Does it change how much sympathy you have for him? Is it possible to respect someone for admitting something this difficult?

a31.quote: our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached.
a31.what: By the early 1990s, 24-hour rolling news was transforming how conflicts and famines were covered. The so-called 'CNN effect' described how graphic television footage could drive public pressure and political action. But this also created intense pressure on journalists to find ever more shocking images — and raised difficult questions about what was appropriate to broadcast into family homes. Alagiah is writing from inside this tension.

a30.quote: We never say so in our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached.
a30.what: 'We never say so in our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached.' Alagiah positions written journalism as more honest than television. This text is framed as the thing TV cannot say — and by admitting it, he invites the reader to trust him precisely because he confesses what others conceal.

a32.quote: To be in a feeding centre is surreptitiously to wipe your hands on the back of your trousers after you've held the clammy palm of a mother who has just cleaned vomit from her child's mouth.
a32.what: 'surreptitiously to wipe your hands on the back of your trousers' — the shift to 'your' places the reader inside the journalist's body, forcing them to confront their own likely instinctive reaction. 'Surreptitiously' is key — the act is shameful, done in secret, even to oneself.

a33.gist: 'Your hands' — are you in the scene?
a33.what: 'surreptitiously to wipe your hands on the back of your trousers' — the second person places you physically in the feeding centre. How does this feel? Does it work as a technique — does it increase your empathy, or does it feel manipulative? What is Alagiah asking you to do by imagining yourself in his position?

a34.quote: they aspire to a dignity that is almost impossible to achieve.
a34.what: 'they aspire to a dignity that is almost impossible to achieve' — dignity and extreme destitution seem irreconcilable, yet Alagiah insists on seeing it. The paradox creates deep respect for the subjects while acknowledging the brutality of what has been done to them.

a36.quote: An old woman will cover her shrivelled body with a soiled cloth as your gaze turns towards her. Or the old and dying man who keeps his hoe next to the mat with which, one day soon, they will shroud his corpse, as if he means to go out and till the soil once all this is over.
a36.what: Two brief images as symbols of human persistence. The man's hoe is especially powerful — kept beside the mat that will soon serve as his shroud, it represents a refusal to abandon the possibility of a future.

a35.quote: An old woman will cover her shrivelled body with a soiled cloth as your gaze turns towards her. Or the old and dying man who keeps his hoe next to the mat with which, one day soon, they will shroud his corpse, as if he means to go out and till the soil once all this is over.
a35.what: The two brief vignettes — the woman covering herself, the man with his hoe — show Alagiah's defining quality as a narrator: he insists on seeing the full humanity of people even in extremity. He could focus only on suffering; instead he notices persistence and pride.

a37.gist: The hoe — what does it make you feel?
a37.what: The man keeps his hoe beside the mat that will become his shroud. He is dying, and he knows it — and yet he keeps the tool he would use if he recovered. What does this image make you feel? How does Alagiah want you to respond to these people — as victims, or as something else?

a38.quote: I saw that face for only a few seconds, a fleeting meeting of eyes before the face turned away, as its owner retreated into the darkness of another hut.
a38.what: 'I saw that face for only a few seconds, a fleeting meeting of eyes' — the language becomes careful and deliberate here, slowing the account down. Alagiah's voice shifts from the overwhelming accumulation of horror to something intimate and puzzled. He is trying to understand something rather than simply record it.

a39.quote: It was not a smile of greeting, it was not a smile of joy — how could it be? — but it was a smile nonetheless.
a39.what: 'It was not a smile of greeting, it was not a smile of joy — how could it be? — but it was a smile nonetheless.' Repeated negatives work through possibilities toward something the writer cannot yet explain. The parenthetical 'how could it be?' is a rare moment of direct editorial comment.

a40.quote: It touched me in a way I could not explain. It moved me in a way that went beyond pity or revulsion.
a40.gist: The unexplained smile — what do you think it means?
a40.what: Before reading on — what do you make of the smile? Alagiah tells us he could not explain it. What possibilities occur to you? How does it feel to be given a detail that resists easy interpretation — does it intrigue you, frustrate you, or draw you in further?

a41.quote: What was it about that smile? I had to find out.
a41.what: 'What was it about that smile? I had to find out.' The short questions break the reflective mode and show the journalist as active enquirer. Alagiah's professional instinct is not suppressed here; it is redirected toward understanding rather than merely recording.

a42.quote: 'It's just that he was embarrassed to be found in this condition,' the translator explained.
a42.what: 'It's just that he was embarrassed to be found in this condition.' The answer is devastating in its simplicity. The word 'just' is striking — the man presents his embarrassment as the most natural thing in the world, which makes the power inversion all the more complete.

a43.quote: And then it clicked. That's what the smile had been about. It was the feeble smile that goes with apology, the kind of smile you might give if you felt you had done something wrong.
a43.gist: The revelation — does it surprise you?
a43.what: The man is embarrassed — not angry, not despairing, not resigned. Embarrassed. Does this surprise you? What assumptions about how people in extreme poverty feel or behave does it challenge? How does Alagiah want you to feel at this moment — about the man, about yourself, about the act of observing suffering?

a44.quote: Normally inured to stories of suffering, accustomed to the evidence of deprivation, I was unsettled by this one smile in a way I had never been before.
a44.what: 'Normally inured to stories of suffering' — Alagiah openly names his own professional numbness before describing how this moment broke through it. This is the ethical turning point of the whole piece — the moment the professional shield fails and something gets through.

a45.quote: The journalist observes, the subject is observed. The journalist is active, the subject is passive.
a45.what: 'The journalist observes, the subject is observed. The journalist is active, the subject is passive.' Three paired antitheses describe an unequal relationship with almost legalistic precision — which is exactly what the smile has just dismantled.

a46.quote: But this smile had turned the tables on that tacit agreement.
a46.gist: Power reversal — the subject gains agency
a46.what: 'But this smile had turned the tables on that tacit agreement.' Alagiah recognises that the man has broken the expected dynamic — without speaking, he has asked a question that Alagiah cannot answer. The journalist, the one with power, has been made to feel accountable.

a47.quote: between the rich world and the poor world.
a47.what: 'between me and him, between us and them, between the rich world and the poor world' — three phrases expanding from personal to global. The individual encounter becomes representative of a vast systemic inequality.

a49.gist: Kevin Carter and the ethics of disaster journalism
a49.what: Photographer Kevin Carter won the 1994 Pulitzer Prize for an image of a starving Sudanese child being stalked by a vulture. He was widely condemned for not intervening to help. Carter died by suicide months after winning the prize. Alagiah is implicitly asking the same question of himself here — the journalist who observes suffering rather than alleviating it. It was a question that haunted the whole profession in the 1990s.

a48.quote: If he was embarrassed to be found weakened by hunger and ground down by conflict, how should I feel to be standing there so strong and confident?
a48.gist: The question the man asks — what is it?
a48.what: 'The man had posed a question' — but he never speaks. What is the question? Alagiah gestures at it: 'If he was embarrassed to be found weakened... how should I feel to be standing there so strong and confident?' Do you think this is the right question? Does it make you think about your own position as someone reading this account from comfort and safety?

a50.quote: I resolved there and then that I would write the story of Gufgaduud with all the power and purpose I could muster.
a50.what: 'I resolved there and then that I would write the story of Gufgaduud with all the power and purpose I could muster.' Writing is framed as the journalist's only available moral response. This is Alagiah's answer to the man's implied question — not action, not intervention, but witness.

a51.quote: It seemed at the time, and still does, the only adequate answer a reporter can give to the man's question.
a51.gist: Is writing enough? What do you think?
a51.what: Alagiah says writing the story is 'the only adequate answer a reporter can give'. Do you agree? Is bearing witness — writing about suffering — a sufficient moral response? Or does it leave you feeling that more should be done? How does this conclusion sit with the picture of journalists 'hunting' for shocking images in ¶3?

a52.quote: Having searched through my notes and studied the dispatch that the BBC broadcast, I see that I never found out what the man's name was.
a52.what: 'I see that I never found out what the man's name was.' This echoes the naming of Amina, Habiba and Ayaan in ¶4 — there, Alagiah gave names to assert humanity. Here, he admits he failed to do the same for the man who affected him most profoundly. The irony is quiet and devastating.

a53.quote: Yet meeting him was a seminal moment in the gradual collection of experiences we call context. Facts and figures are the easy part of journalism. Knowing where they sit in the great scheme of things is much harder.
a53.what: 'the gradual collection of experiences we call context' — a quietly extraordinary phrase. Alagiah is describing how journalists build understanding, but the word 'call' implies a slight scepticism about the label. Is 'context' the right word for what this man gave him?

a54.quote: my nameless friend, if you are still alive, I owe you one.
a54.what: 'my nameless friend, if you are still alive, I owe you one.' A direct address to the man — intimate and quietly devastating. 'If you are still alive' acknowledges the real probability that he is not. 'I owe you one' is startlingly colloquial: raw, unguarded, genuine.

a55.gist: The final line — what does it leave you with?
a55.what: 'I owe you one' — an informal, almost throwaway phrase to end a serious piece of writing. How does this tonal shift affect you? What does it suggest about Alagiah's feelings for the man? And what does 'if you are still alive' add — why not simply 'wherever you are'? What does ending on that uncertainty do to you as a reader?
